status: DRAFT — coach approval pending; not validated for live classroom/team use
ownership: Anthony Boyd / Worldmedia Publishing & Consulting LLC
notes: Coach-specific definitions are proposed teaching language, not a quotation from or endorsement by a specific coach.
Shell Defense is represented as a shell drill rather than mischaracterized as a separate defense system.
Communication Calls is an umbrella training entry; its breakdown into separate terms needs coach approval.
No-middle and pack-line are separate scheme concepts and may have different forcing rules.
Motion Steps have not been added as full animations; all new diagrams are static until reviewed.
Existing five IDs must remain stable; saved coach edits must survive upgrades.
All diagrams depict representative teaching scenes, not a single universal scheme.
Six additional pre-existing defensive coverages (Over, Under, High Drop, Low Drop, Ice/Down, Weak) are revised in the full defensive study pool, without increasing the total term count.

researchSources.title: Jr. NBA – Fundamentals of Stunt and Recover
Online Basketball Playbook – Defensive Ball Screens

existingRevisions.definition: The deepest weak-side help defender nearest the basket, responsible for protecting the rim and often delaying a rolling screener before the team rotates.
existingRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Identify the low man early, tag the roller when required by our scheme, then call the next rotation and recover or X-out on the pass.
existingRevisions.cue: Call 'low!' or the team's agreed help call; protect the rim, then find the next matchup.
existingRevisions.commonMistake: Watching the ball while the roller slips behind, or tagging with no planned recovery.
existingRevisions.diagramNote: X3 starts on the weak-side baseline, steps into the roller's path and communicates coverage behind the ball screen.

quizReview.prompt: The roller breaks free down the lane. Which defender is commonly responsible for the first weak-side tag?
quizReview.correctResponse: The low man, subject to the team's help rules.
distractors: The ball handler's primary on-ball defender.
The screener's defender nearest half court.
The first defender who calls a timeout.

existingRevisions.definition: A ball-screen coverage in which the screener's defender retreats to protect the basket and the on-ball defender fights over or through the screen to recover.
existingRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Keep the ball between the two defenders. The big communicates depth; the guard reconnects from behind without conceding a layup.
existingRevisions.cue: Big: call 'drop'; contain the drive and roller. Guard: fight through and recover to the ball.
existingRevisions.commonMistake: The big backs all the way to the rim without addressing the ball, or the guard dies on the screen.
existingRevisions.diagramNote: X5 retreats in the lane while X1 chases the ball handler over the screen; they protect the rim and pocket pass together.

quizReview.prompt: What must the on-ball defender do when their teammate is playing drop coverage?
quizReview.correctResponse: Navigate the screen and recover to the ball handler.
distractors: Immediately abandon the handler and guard the corner.
Switch automatically without calling it.
Double-team the ball alone after the screen.

existingRevisions.definition: A coverage in which two defenders exchange offensive assignments as a screen arrives to stay connected without a long chase.
existingRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Call the exchange early and make both matchups explicit. X5 takes the handler while X1 takes the screener; anticipate the roll and any mismatch.
existingRevisions.cue: Call 'switch' early; one defender takes the ball and the other takes the screener.
existingRevisions.commonMistake: Both defenders follow the ball or neither claims the rolling screener, creating an open lane.
existingRevisions.diagramNote: X5 steps toward the handler as X1 turns and picks up the screener; two defensive assignments swap clearly.

quizReview.prompt: After switching a ball screen, who guards the screener?
quizReview.correctResponse: The defender who was guarding the ball before the switch.
distractors: The defender who was originally guarding the screener.
The nearest weak-side corner defender.
Nobody; both defenders stay with the ball.

existingRevisions.definition: A ball-screen coverage in which the screener's defender temporarily steps out to disrupt the ball handler and then recovers to the screener.
existingRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Call the show, get in the ball handler's path without fouling, and sprint back when the guard recovers; weak-side help protects the roller.
existingRevisions.cue: Big: show high, slow the ball, and recover. Guard: fight over and reconnect.
existingRevisions.commonMistake: Showing without recovering, or leaving the roller unprotected after the hedge.
existingRevisions.diagramNote: X5 moves toward the dribble above the screen, then recovers to the rolling 5; X1 continues over.

quizReview.prompt: What happens after a screener's defender hedges?
quizReview.correctResponse: Recover to their original matchup while the on-ball defender reconnects.
distractors: Stay with the ball handler for the rest of the possession.
Stop at the screen and wait for a timeout.
Abandon the roller and rotate to the opposite corner.

existingRevisions.definition: An aggressive ball-screen coverage in which two defenders attack the ball handler together to force a quick pass, retreat, or turnover.
existingRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: X1 and X5 arrive together with active hands and legal spacing; the remaining three defenders rotate to cover the first pass and protect the rim.
existingRevisions.cue: Call 'blitz'; trap together and rotate behind the pressure.
existingRevisions.commonMistake: One defender attacks early while the other stays back, leaving a clear escape and an uncovered roller.
existingRevisions.diagramNote: X1 and X5 converge on the ball after the screen, with the weak-side defenders covering the passing lanes and roll.

quizReview.prompt: When two defenders blitz the ball, what must the other defenders do?
quizReview.correctResponse: Rotate behind the trap to cover the roller and passing outlets.
distractors: Keep all five defenders on their original players without shifting.
Send a third defender to trap and leave the rim vacant.
Run back to half court before locating an outlet.

newEntries.definition: A team-defense teaching drill in which players shift between guarding the ball, denying a pass, and helping away from the ball as passes move around the perimeter.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: In a 4-on-4 shell, freeze after each pass to check ball-you-player vision, help gaps, low-man positioning and controlled closeouts; add live drives gradually.
newEntries.cue: Call 'ball', 'deny' and 'help'; move on the pass, not after the catch.
newEntries.commonMistake: Standing still off the ball or losing sight of the assigned player during a rotation.
newEntries.diagramNote: Four offensive spots on the perimeter with four matching defenders: X1 pressures the ball, X2 is a pass away, X3 and X4 are in help positions.

quizReview.prompt: The ball moves from the top to the wing during shell drill. When should off-ball defenders adjust?
quizReview.correctResponse: While the pass is moving, before the catch.
distractors: Only when the passer has taken their next dribble.
After the receiver already starts driving.
Only after a coach yells stop.

newEntries.definition: The controlled approach a defender uses to reach a shooter or receiver, contest a shot and stay balanced against a drive.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Sprint most of the distance, decelerate under control with active hands and balanced feet, then take away the direction required by the team's scheme.
newEntries.cue: Sprint, brake, contest, contain; arrive ready to slide.
newEntries.commonMistake: Flying past the shooter or chopping too early and allowing an uncontested shot.
newEntries.diagramNote: X2 closes from help toward offensive 2 at the wing and stops short in a balanced guarding stance.

quizReview.prompt: Why does a defender slow down at the end of a closeout?
quizReview.correctResponse: To contest without giving up an immediate drive.
distractors: To avoid contesting the ball at all.
To set a screen for the receiver.
To turn and run toward the baseline.

newEntries.definition: Off-ball positioning that places a defender ready to support a teammate when the ball is on the opposite side, while still tracking their assigned player.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Sink toward the help line when appropriately away from the ball; maintain vision of both ball and matchup and rotate as the ball moves.
newEntries.cue: See ball and player; step toward the lane when you are the weak-side helper.
newEntries.commonMistake: Face-guarding the matchup so completely that the helper cannot see penetration.
newEntries.diagramNote: X3 drops toward the lane as offensive 1 controls the ball on the opposite wing.

quizReview.prompt: Where should a weak-side defender look when positioned to help?
quizReview.correctResponse: Keep the ball and their assigned player in view.
distractors: Watch only their own player and ignore the ball.
Face the bench until their player cuts.
Look only at the offensive rebounders.

newEntries.definition: A temporary bump, body presence or path interruption by a help defender that slows the screener rolling toward the rim.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: The assigned helper contacts only legally, meets the roll early, communicates the tag and releases into the required next rotation or recovery.
newEntries.cue: Tag the roller early; call the handoff and recover or rotate on the pass.
newEntries.commonMistake: Tagging too late or standing on the roller and surrendering an open corner shooter.
newEntries.diagramNote: X3 crosses from the weak-side gap to meet rolling 5, then must rotate to a perimeter matchup.

quizReview.prompt: Why does a help defender tag a rolling screener?
quizReview.correctResponse: To delay the roll and buy time for the primary coverage and rotation.
distractors: To keep a teammate away from the basket.
To give the ball handler an open passing lane.
To deny all three-point shots without rotating.

newEntries.definition: A brief aggressive step toward the ball or driving lane that makes the ball handler hesitate, followed by a quick return to the original matchup.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Stunt far enough to influence the drive or passing lane, then recover before the offense can exploit the abandoned shooter.
newEntries.cue: Show help, then sprint back under control.
newEntries.commonMistake: Fully committing to the ball and giving up an easy catch-and-shoot opportunity.
newEntries.diagramNote: X2 jabs into the lane toward driving 1, then returns to guard shooter 2.

quizReview.prompt: After the stunt forces a hesitation, what is the defender's next responsibility?
quizReview.correctResponse: Recover to the original assignment unless a team rotation is called.
distractors: Become an extra permanent on-ball defender.
Sprint to the opposite baseline and remain there.
Switch onto the screener automatically.

newEntries.definition: A brief swipe or jab by a nearby perimeter defender toward a post player's dribble to disrupt rhythm without abandoning the perimeter assignment.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Dig on the post dribble with active hands, communicate the help and retreat to the shooter without recklessly reaching or fouling.
newEntries.cue: Dig on the dribble; get back to the shooter.
newEntries.commonMistake: Reaching across the post player's body or lingering in the paint while a shooter stands open.
newEntries.diagramNote: X2 momentarily steps from the wing toward post player 5's dribble, then recovers to offensive 2.

quizReview.prompt: When is a short dig at the post most often timed?
quizReview.correctResponse: When the post player puts the ball on the floor.
distractors: Before the entry pass leaves the point guard's hands.
Only once the shot is already in the air.
After the post player has passed out and the ball is gone.

newEntries.definition: Positioning by an off-ball defender in the space between offensive players so they can discourage a drive while staying close enough to recover.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Sit in the driving gap according to team rules, show early help, then close out under control if the pass goes to the matchup.
newEntries.cue: Own the driving gap and recover on the pass.
newEntries.commonMistake: Hugging a non-shooter too tightly and leaving the lane open, or helping so deep that recovery is impossible.
newEntries.diagramNote: X2 shifts into the gap between driving 1 and wing receiver 2, then recovers toward 2.

quizReview.prompt: Why does a gap defender shade toward the ball?
quizReview.correctResponse: To discourage straight-line penetration while remaining able to recover.
distractors: To allow a direct layup while denying every pass.
To screen the shooter for their teammate.
To avoid ever closing out to their original player.

newEntries.definition: Help positioned near the center of the free-throw line, often called the nail, to deter a drive into the middle and support ball-screen coverage.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: The designated nail helper moves early to the free-throw line center, communicates penetration and knows whether to stunt or rotate fully.
newEntries.cue: Touch the nail area early; stop the middle without losing the next pass.
newEntries.commonMistake: Arriving after the driver reaches the free-throw line or never identifying the next shooter.
newEntries.diagramNote: X4 slides from the weak-side slot to the free-throw-line nail as 1 drives toward the middle.

quizReview.prompt: Where on the court is the 'nail'?
quizReview.correctResponse: At the middle of the free-throw line.
distractors: The midpoint of the half-court line.
The corner of the backboard.
A spot outside the sideline at the scorer's table.

newEntries.definition: A help rotation in which an on-ball defender who has been beaten peels off the driver to take a teammate's vacated assignment while the teammate contains the ball.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Call the peel clearly: the helper takes the dribbler and the beaten defender immediately picks up the helper's matchup; do not chase the same ball.
newEntries.cue: When beaten, peel to the open matchup as your helper contains the drive.
newEntries.commonMistake: Both defenders chase the driver, leaving the helper's original player open.
newEntries.diagramNote: X2 leaves wing 2 to contain a penetrating 1; beaten X1 peels away to cover 2.

quizReview.prompt: After a helper stops the drive on a peel switch, what does the beaten on-ball defender do?
quizReview.correctResponse: Leave the ball and pick up the helper's vacated assignment.
distractors: Keep chasing the handler alongside the helper.
Run to the bench for a substitution.
Automatically trap the ball with no rotation.

newEntries.definition: A two-defender scramble rotation in which defenders exchange coverage of a wing and corner after help or a drive-and-kick, creating crossing recovery paths.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Identify the pass sequence and communicate who takes the first receiver and who closes to the second, avoiding two defenders on one shooter.
newEntries.cue: Call 'X-out'; first defender closes, second covers the next pass.
newEntries.commonMistake: Both defenders closing to the same shooter and leaving the next receiver open.
newEntries.diagramNote: X3 closes from the lane to the corner while X2 rotates across to the wing, making crossing paths.

quizReview.prompt: What problem does an X-out rotation solve?
quizReview.correctResponse: It covers two perimeter passing options after a defender has helped in the lane.
distractors: Both defenders stay in the paint regardless of passes.
The closest big guards every perimeter shooter.
Both players collapse on the same receiver.

newEntries.definition: An off-ball switch used to remove an unfavorable defender, often a smaller player, from a post mismatch before the offense can exploit it.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: A bigger teammate calls the scram, replaces the small defender on the post player and sends the small defender to the new matchup before the entry pass.
newEntries.cue: Call 'scram' early; swap out of a bad post mismatch.
newEntries.commonMistake: Waiting until the post entry is complete or sending two defenders to the post without a clear exchange.
newEntries.diagramNote: X4 leaves the weak-side slot to take post 5 while smaller X1 escapes from 5 to guard offensive 4.

quizReview.prompt: Why would a defense use a scram switch?
quizReview.correctResponse: To remove an unfavorable mismatch, especially a small defender guarding the post.
distractors: To make a smaller defender guard a bigger post scorer.
To prevent a teammate from closing out on any shooter.
To force a ball-screen trap with no post defender.

newEntries.definition: An off-ball denial technique in which a defender positions above a cutter to block their intended route over a screen, often against a dangerous shooter.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Take away the shooter's route to the top of the screen and communicate the backdoor cut that this pressure can invite.
newEntries.cue: Sit on the high side of the cutter; call out the backdoor risk.
newEntries.commonMistake: Overplaying the top without a teammate protecting the backdoor lane.
newEntries.diagramNote: X2 positions between shooter 2 and the upper screen route; offensive 2 may counter with a backdoor cut.

quizReview.prompt: What is the main risk when a defender top-locks an off-ball shooter?
quizReview.correctResponse: A backdoor cut behind the overplaying defender.
distractors: The shooter must remain stationary outside the arc.
The defender is forced to guard the referee.
The screener becomes an automatic ball handler.

newEntries.definition: A team defensive rule or scheme designed to keep ball handlers out of the middle of the floor, commonly by influencing perimeter drives toward the sideline or baseline.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Angle the on-ball stance to deny the middle and coordinate low help and next-pass rotations; team details differ and must be confirmed.
newEntries.cue: No middle; send the drive toward the help the team has assigned.
newEntries.commonMistake: Forcing baseline without the backline help being ready, or allowing an easy middle drive.
newEntries.diagramNote: X1 shades driver 1 toward the sideline while X3 prepares to protect a baseline drive.

quizReview.prompt: In a no-middle scheme, which direction is the defender trying to deny?
quizReview.correctResponse: The middle of the floor.
distractors: The sideline and baseline.
The offensive team's bench area.
Every pass outside the three-point line.

newEntries.definition: A player-to-player team defense that pressures the ball while off-ball defenders position inside an imaginary interior boundary to crowd driving lanes and protect the paint.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: One defender pressures the ball; the other defenders stay in help positions inside the pack until passing action requires controlled closeouts. Do not confuse it with a no-middle forcing scheme.
newEntries.cue: Pressure the ball; pack the driving lanes; close out on passes.
newEntries.commonMistake: Over-denying away from the ball and opening straight-line drives into the paint.
newEntries.diagramNote: X1 pressures ball 1 while X2, X3 and X4 sit inside a compact shell along the paint and elbows.

quizReview.prompt: What is the off-ball priority in pack-line defense?
quizReview.correctResponse: Crowd driving lanes in help positions, then close out on the pass.
distractors: Deny every pass at full court regardless of ball position.
Leave driving lanes open while trapping the weak side.
Stay at the rim and never close out on passes.

newEntries.definition: Legal positioning after a shot that keeps an opponent from taking a direct path to an offensive rebound, followed by pursuit of the ball.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: On the shot, find your opponent, establish inside positioning with balanced body contact when legal, then release to secure the rebound.
newEntries.cue: Shot up: find, make contact legally, then go get the ball.
newEntries.commonMistake: Watching the shot without locating an opponent, or using an illegal push to create space.
newEntries.diagramNote: X5 seals offensive 5 away from the rim while teammates locate other rebounders and pursue the shot.

quizReview.prompt: What happens after a defender establishes a box-out position?
quizReview.correctResponse: Pursue and secure the rebound.
distractors: Run away from the ball to start the fast break.
Watch the shot until the opponent gets the rebound.
Hold or push the opponent illegally instead of pursuing.

newEntries.definition: Short, consistent spoken signals that tell teammates about the ball, help, screens, switches, cutters and rotations so the team responds together.
newEntries.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Teach a small shared call vocabulary, such as 'ball', 'help', 'screen left', 'switch', 'stay', and 'shot'; confirm exact calls with the coach.
newEntries.cue: Talk early, loud and specific: ball, help, screen, switch, shot.
newEntries.commonMistake: Using vague late calls, or two defenders issuing conflicting coverage instructions.
newEntries.diagramNote: Five defenders communicate from assigned floor spots; X1 calls ball, X2 calls screen, X3 calls help, X4 calls the next rotation.

quizReview.prompt: What makes a useful defensive communication call?
quizReview.correctResponse: Early, clear information that teammates can act on.
distractors: A call that comes only after the play finishes.
A secret term that no teammate understands.
Shouting continuously without identifying the action.

supplementalCoverageRevisions.definition: A ball-screen coverage in which the on-ball defender fights over the top of the screen to stay attached to a shooting or driving ball handler.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Navigate tight over the screen, communicate to the big and reconnect to pressure the handler from behind.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.cue: Call 'over', get skinny past the screen and rear contest without fouling.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.commonMistake: Going wide around the screen and letting the ball handler turn the corner uncontested.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.diagramNote: X1 navigates above the screen and chases 1; the big provides the next defensive layer.

quizReview.prompt: When going over a ball screen, what is the on-ball defender trying to do?
quizReview.correctResponse: Stay attached to the handler by navigating above the screen.
distractors: Leave the handler and guard a corner shooter.
Run under the screen and concede every three.
Switch without a call regardless of the plan.

supplementalCoverageRevisions.definition: A ball-screen coverage where the on-ball defender travels underneath the screen to protect the drive against a less threatening outside shooter.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Go under quickly, meet the handler on the other side, and contest if the handler becomes a shooting threat.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.cue: Call 'under'; beat the ball to the far side and recover into a stance.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.commonMistake: Drifting too deep under the screen and conceding an uncontested pull-up shot.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.diagramNote: X1 passes below the screener and recovers in front of 1; teammates communicate the gap.

quizReview.prompt: What is the main risk of choosing to go under against a strong shooter?
quizReview.correctResponse: The handler can stop and shoot behind the screen.
distractors: The screener always becomes the on-ball defender.
The defense automatically earns possession.
The ball handler must pass to the corner.

supplementalCoverageRevisions.definition: A drop variation in which the screener's defender begins higher toward the ball-screen level before retreating to protect the rim and roller.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Start near the screen level, stay balanced between the ball and roller, then retreat on the drive while the guard reconnects.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.cue: Big: show at the higher drop point, then retreat and contain the paint.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.commonMistake: Staying stranded above the screen and giving the roller a free lane to the rim.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.diagramNote: X5 begins near the screen instead of deep in the lane, then drops as the guard fights through.

quizReview.prompt: What distinguishes high drop from a deeper low drop?
quizReview.correctResponse: The big begins closer to the level of the screen.
distractors: Both defenders must trap above half court.
The guard refuses to navigate the screen.
The big guards the opposite corner immediately.

supplementalCoverageRevisions.definition: A deeper form of drop coverage in which the screener's defender stays closer to the basket to prioritize rim and rolling-lane protection.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Maintain a low but active stance to contain the drive and roller while the guard recovers to challenge open pull-ups.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.cue: Big: stay low and protect the rim; guard: reconnect and contest the pull-up.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.commonMistake: Standing flat-footed under the rim while both the roller and ball handler arrive unchallenged.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.diagramNote: X5 begins closer to the rim than in high drop, while X1 must fight back into the play.

quizReview.prompt: What is a primary trade-off of a low drop position?
quizReview.correctResponse: More rim protection but more space for a pull-up jumper.
distractors: Less rim protection and no possible driving lane.
An automatic switch of both defenders.
An immediate full-court double team.

supplementalCoverageRevisions.definition: A side ball-screen coverage that denies use of the screen by influencing the ball handler toward the sideline or baseline and away from the middle.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: The guard denies the screen with the high-side angle; the big positions below it to contain the forced-side drive.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.cue: Call 'ice'; deny the screen and send the ball into prepared baseline help.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.commonMistake: Forcing the ball toward baseline without the second defender and low help ready to contain it.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.diagramNote: X1 jumps to the screen-side shoulder to deny the screen while X5 waits below the screen.

quizReview.prompt: What is the basic aim of ICE on a side ball screen?
quizReview.correctResponse: Deny the screen and direct the handler toward sideline/baseline help.
distractors: Invite a middle drive before the screen arrives.
Switch all five defenders to the nearest player.
Leave the corner defender to pressure half court.

supplementalCoverageRevisions.definition: A defensive influence or coverage call that steers the ball handler toward a less effective hand or predetermined help area according to the team's rules.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.coachDefinition: PROPOSED — coach review required: Know the scouting direction and help-side support; shade the handler without surrendering an easier direct lane.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.cue: Call the agreed weak-side force; shade the handler toward the planned help.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.commonMistake: Guessing the force direction and opening the middle or baseline without support.
supplementalCoverageRevisions.diagramNote: X1 shades the handler toward the scouting-agreed weaker hand while other defenders prepare help.

quizReview.prompt: Before forcing a handler 'weak', what must the on-ball defender know?
quizReview.correctResponse: The agreed force direction and where the help is positioned.
distractors: Only the opponent's jersey number.
Whether the referee has stopped the clock.
Which teammate will take the next free throw.
